title: Set Context Log
user: A self-directed lifter who needs to record what changed a set—not just weight and reps—so the next workout has usable context.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The self-hosted workout-tracker discussion drew 14 comments; a user explicitly called out the missing Apple Health import and another requested privacy-friendly wearable handling.
Requester needs notes on individual sets such as ‘grip slipped,’ ‘paused reps,’ and ‘felt easy, increase next time’; session-level notes are insufficient.

recurrence: Two independent fitness-tracker communities in 2025–26; the pain occurs every training session and destroys the decision context needed for progressive overload.
current_workaround: Put a cryptic note in a phone app or general notes app, or remember it until the next session.
incumbents_and_gap: Wger, Hevy, and Strong store structured sets, but the cited Wger request shows set-level qualitative context is still an afterthought; generic notes do not surface it when repeating the lift.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a fast set row (weight, reps, RPE, one-tap caveat), a next-session recall card, and CSV/JSON export. Non-goals: workout programming marketplace, social feed, wearable sync, nutrition logging.
success_measure: In a 14-day pilot, at least 60% of logged working sets include a context marker and 70% of repeat exercises open the prior-set recall card.
monetization: one-time — personal data stays on device and the utility has no recurring infrastructure need.
constraints: Store health/fitness data locally by default; make exports portable; no medical claims; accommodate kg/lb per entry rather than silently converting history.
why_distinct: It is a decision-memory layer for lifting, not another exercise catalog or AI workout generator.

title: Freezer Life Ledger
user: A household cook who freezes part of packages and needs to know what is open, frozen, and worth using first.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 Show HN launched PPantry specifically as an offline-first pantry and inventory tracker, confirming active demand for a private pantry workflow.
Grocy users must manually mark a remainder as opened after consuming part of a package; the issue asks for that state transition to be automatic.

recurrence: Independent pantry users are building and requesting workflows around the same repeated event: open a package, use part, freeze or store the rest.
current_workaround: Write dates on bags, keep a rough freezer list, or perform several manual stock state changes in Grocy.
incumbents_and_gap: Grocy is powerful but its request illustrates inventory-model friction; PPantry validates offline demand, yet neither evidence source resolves the low-effort package-lifecycle moment.
smallest_useful_product: Barcode/name entry, one-tap Open/Freeze/Finish actions, best-before date, location, and a ‘use next’ list. Non-goals: retailer integrations, recipe scraping, nutrition calculations, multi-user accounts.
success_measure: At least 50% of households still have 15+ active package records after 30 days, with fewer than 20% marked ‘unknown state.’
monetization: one-time — useful offline with no server dependency.
constraints: Local IndexedDB with export/import; no food-safety guarantees; dates are user-entered reminders, not safety advice.
why_distinct: Models the state of an opened package rather than trying to be a complete pantry, grocery, recipe, and nutrition suite.

title: Pantry Meal Gap
user: A home cook deciding dinner from imperfect on-hand ingredients who needs to see the smallest missing shopping list, not an idealized recipe catalog.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker released an iOS app that photographs a pantry and tells the user what they can cook—a direct attempt to solve on-hand meal choice.
Tandoor’s ‘Currently On Hand’ search filter was reported as having no effect, showing this ingredient-availability decision is a meaningful product surface.

recurrence: Two current products independently center cooking around what is physically available; failure of the on-hand filter makes the task immediately frustrating.
current_workaround: Search recipes, mentally substitute ingredients, then make an ad-hoc grocery list.
incumbents_and_gap: Tandoor and Mealie organize recipes; pantry-camera apps identify items. The gap is a fast, editable shortage calculation that tolerates substitutions and partial quantities.
smallest_useful_product: Local ingredient list, 20 manually entered staple meals, match score, acceptable substitutions, and auto-generated missing-items list. Non-goals: image recognition, web recipe scraping, grocery delivery, meal-plan AI.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, users choose a meal from the tool at least twice weekly and accept the generated missing list without editing in 60% of uses.
monetization: free — a small local utility needs a low-friction adoption wedge before any paid expansion.
constraints: No copyrighted recipe ingestion; users enter their own meal templates; quantities and allergy suitability are user responsibility.
why_distinct: It answers ‘what can I make with one small gap?’ rather than generating recipes or maintaining a full food database.

title: Recipe Measure Check
user: A cook importing or typing a personal recipe who needs ambiguous dual units turned into a reviewable shopping and cooking checklist.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The recipe-app Show HN generated 74 comments; commenters asked what it offered beyond popular recipe trackers and reported search/browser failures, underscoring that feature breadth alone is not enough.
Tandoor’s ingredient parser mishandles real dual-measurement inputs such as ‘4 tbsp/58 grams’ and ‘1½ cups (210 grams).’

recurrence: Recipe applications repeatedly encounter the same unglamorous input-normalization issue; it blocks the practical handoff from a personal recipe to shopping/cooking.
current_workaround: Leave the messy text untouched, manually rewrite quantities, or trust a parser that silently loses a measurement.
incumbents_and_gap: Tandoor and recipe trackers optimize storage and discovery; their parser issue shows a gap for a tiny, review-first measurement normalizer rather than another hosted recipe database.
smallest_useful_product: Paste or type ingredient lines; highlight ambiguous pairs, let the user pick display/shopping unit, keep original text, and export a clean checklist. Non-goals: scraping publishers, nutrition estimates, recipe sharing, LLM recipe creation.
success_measure: At least 85% of imported ingredient lines are accepted or corrected in one pass, and users export a checklist for 10+ recipes in the first month.
monetization: one-time — private local conversion utility with no ongoing service cost.
constraints: Preserve original user-entered text; no automated copying from copyrighted sites; unit conversions must be transparent and editable.
why_distinct: A constrained quality-control tool for the recipe people already own, not a recipe-content clone or an AI wrapper.

title: Caregiver Last Action
user: Two or more baby caregivers handing off feed, sleep, medicine, and diaper timing who need one unambiguous answer to ‘what happened last, and when did it end?’

evidence.quote_or_summary: PoopyFeed was introduced as self-hosted baby tracking for feedings, diapers, and naps, validating a privacy-conscious niche for event logging.
A Baby Buddy user requests that ‘time since last feeding’ use the end time rather than start time—a small detail with direct handoff consequences.

recurrence: Separate baby-tracking communities focus on the same frequent, high-stakes handoff data; timing semantics matter several times a day.
current_workaround: Text a partner, check a shared app timeline, or infer from memory while tired.
incumbents_and_gap: Baby Buddy and self-hosted trackers are broad logs. The gap is an ultra-fast, shared ‘last action’ display with explicit start/end semantics and no analytics burden.
smallest_useful_product: A locally synced PWA for two devices: one-tap event start/stop, prominent last-action board, correction history, and encrypted QR pairing. Non-goals: medical guidance, developmental predictions, cloud accounts, community features.
success_measure: Paired caregivers record 80% of feed/sleep events in the app for seven consecutive days and resolve a handoff lookup in under 10 seconds in usability tests.
monetization: one-time — a short but intense family lifecycle, with privacy favoring no account.
constraints: Treat data as sensitive family/health-adjacent data; encrypted local pairing; no medical recommendations; reliable conflict handling is mandatory.
why_distinct: A handoff instrument, not a full baby journal; the product deliberately privileges the next caregiver’s immediate question.

title: Home Handoff Board
user: A household that needs to coordinate recurring chores, meals, and appointments in a five-minute weekly handoff without inviting everyone into an account system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker described an open-source, no-account family calendar used by their whole household, a direct local-first validation.
Tandoor’s current ‘Household Object Ownership Issue’ shows that even a recipe/planning system must explicitly resolve what belongs to a shared household.

recurrence: Current family-calendar work and a 2026 shared-household ownership issue converge on the same need: household work needs clear, shared boundaries rather than an individual to-do list.
current_workaround: Shared calendar plus chat messages plus a separate chore app, with no common ‘this week’ handoff view.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, Cozi, Tandoor, and household organizers each cover part of it. The unresolved gap is a printable/phone-friendly week board that joins time blocks and responsibility without accounts.
smallest_useful_product: Local week board with person-colored cards, duration, repeat rules, meal slots, print view, and QR export/import between household devices. Non-goals: messaging, school integrations, cloud calendar sync, gamified chores.
success_measure: At least 70% of cards scheduled on Sunday are marked done, moved, or explicitly skipped by week end across a four-week test.
monetization: one-time — household coordination data should not require a subscription or account.
constraints: Offline-first sharing must make conflicts visible; avoid collecting children’s data; support printable export and data portability.
why_distinct: It is a bounded weekly coordination artifact, not another general calendar or task-management platform.

title: Room Move Inventory
user: A renter, homeowner, or family moving items between rooms who needs to label, find, and later verify possessions without maintaining a full asset-management system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2025 HN post presented Homely as a combined home-inventory and meal-management app, showing makers still target home inventory as an unmet household workflow.
Homebox users reported being unable to attach an existing barcode to a new item, exposing friction at the exact physical-labeling step.

recurrence: Home-inventory builders and Homebox users independently invest in physical-to-digital capture; the hard moment is tagging an item while moving it, not maintaining a rich catalog later.
current_workaround: Photograph boxes, write labels by hand, maintain a spreadsheet, or abandon detailed inventory after initial setup.
incumbents_and_gap: Homebox is a capable self-hosted asset system; insurance-inventory apps are heavy. The gap is temporary, room-and-box-aware capture with a fast label loop.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile scan/create flow, room and box labels, photo, QR sheet generation, search by scan, and CSV export. Non-goals: insurance valuation, warranties, multi-property administration, cloud OCR.
success_measure: A user can label and record 30 items in under 20 minutes, then locate 80% of a sampled set by scan/search one month later.
monetization: one-time — episodic move/organization utility with no need for hosted storage.
constraints: Keep photos local unless explicitly exported; QR codes must be stable and printable; do not represent the inventory as insurance evidence.
why_distinct: Optimized for the short, physical move-and-find loop rather than becoming a lifetime asset database.

title: Maintenance Proof Book
user: A homeowner who needs a durable record linking a repair, contractor, part, photo, receipt, and next service date.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker built a fair-price checker for home repairs using labor data, evidence that homeowners actively need support around repair decisions rather than generic project boards.
Micasa’s open issue is ‘No ability to link a document with the service log entry,’ directly identifying the missing evidence-to-maintenance connection.

recurrence: The repair-price product and a dedicated home-maintenance project both focus on the same costly lifecycle: decide, repair, document, and remember.
current_workaround: Keep a folder of receipts, photos in a camera roll, and future reminders in a calendar with no shared object history.
incumbents_and_gap: Micasa and Homebox offer broad maintenance/asset workflows; quote checkers address one transaction. The gap is a tiny evidence packet per repair that remains usable at resale, warranty, or repeat service time.
smallest_useful_product: Offline property timeline with repair cards, receipt/photo attachment, part/vendor fields, next-due date, and a single PDF export. Non-goals: contractor marketplace, quote prediction, property management, cloud document storage.
success_measure: At least 75% of a pilot household’s new repair entries include one evidence attachment and a next-action field after 60 days.
monetization: one-time — records should remain accessible for years without a service contract.
constraints: Sensitive address/vendor data stays local; clear storage/export limits; PDF export must preserve attachment provenance without legal-certification claims.
why_distinct: A repair record that proves and schedules a decision, rather than a generic task list or contractor lead-gen funnel.

title: Pocket Reconcile
user: A privacy-minded budgeter who wants to reconcile cash, cards, and a few manual transactions from a phone in two minutes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A budget-app maintainer reported a 2011-origin iOS app; commenters specifically praised its offline capability and sync-after-signal model.
Actual Budget users reported that the mobile Reconcile button does not work, plus formatting problems—reconciliation remains a real mobile workflow rather than a desktop-only detail.

recurrence: An enduring budget app earns praise for offline behavior while a leading local-first budget project receives a mobile reconciliation defect report; both point to the phone moment.
current_workaround: Record spending later, use a calculator plus notes, or open a dense desktop budget interface on a phone.
incumbents_and_gap: Actual, YNAB, and Firefly III are comprehensive finance systems. The gap is an exceptionally small, offline reconcile surface for people who do not want bank linking or full envelope setup.
smallest_useful_product: Local accounts, balance snapshot, quick transactions, count-to-balance reconcile, discrepancy note, and CSV import/export. Non-goals: bank aggregation, investment tracking, tax advice, shared cloud ledger.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot users complete a weekly reconcile on mobile for four consecutive weeks, with median completion under three minutes.
monetization: one-time — local financial records should not require ongoing vendor access.
constraints: No bank credentials or financial advice; encrypted local export option; accurate decimal currency arithmetic and transparent backup recovery.
why_distinct: It deliberately stops at reliable reconciliation rather than competing as a full personal-finance platform.

title: Bill Runway Card
user: A household budgeter who needs to see which bills must be paid before the next payday, including odd weekly or deferred charges.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 Show HN introduced Coinvane as an open-source budgeting application, another fresh attempt at personal budgeting rather than evidence of a solved category.
Firefly III users request management of incoming invoices that must be paid later, a distinct cash-timing problem from recording a completed transaction.

recurrence: New open-source budgeting launches and a mature finance project’s open invoice request show that cash timing remains poorly served inside general ledgers.
current_workaround: Calendar reminders, sticky notes, a spreadsheet, or mentally reserve money in a checking account.
incumbents_and_gap: Coinvane, Actual, and Firefly III focus on ledgers and budgets. The gap is one plain-language card answering ‘what is already committed before my next income date?’ including weekly and irregular cadence.
smallest_useful_product: Offline bill cards with due date/cadence, expected amount/range, next-payday marker, paid toggle, and a printable two-week runway. Non-goals: bank sync, credit scoring, bill payment, debt advice.
success_measure: In a six-week pilot, users record 90% of known recurring/deferred bills and report zero surprise due dates that were already in scope.
monetization: one-time — it holds personal commitments locally without requiring a financial-data service.
constraints: No payment initiation or financial advice; explicit handling for estimates and currency; local backup/export is essential.
why_distinct: A cash-commitment horizon, not another transaction categorizer or subscription cancellation service.

title: Season Gap Garden
user: A small-space food gardener who wants to spot an empty bed window and choose a simple follow-on crop from their own past planting notes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Leaftide launched as a garden planner with climate-aware scheduling, showing current demand for time-aware rather than purely visual garden planning.
Open Garden Planner has an active request for succession-plan tools: find succession gaps, suggest successors, and persist a succession plan.

recurrence: Two 2026 garden-planning efforts independently prioritize scheduling and succession, not just drawing beds.
current_workaround: Draw a bed plan, keep planting dates in a notebook, and manually work out what can follow a harvested crop.
incumbents_and_gap: Leaftide and Open Garden Planner are broad planners. The gap is a light, personal ‘gap’ view based on only the gardener’s bed dates and chosen crop durations—no giant plant encyclopedia required.
smallest_useful_product: Offline bed list, sow/transplant/expected-clear dates, a calendar strip showing open windows, user-defined successor templates, and season CSV export. Non-goals: weather prediction, plant marketplace, companion-plant claims, automated agronomy.
success_measure: After one season, at least 50% of planted beds have a recorded next crop or intentional rest period, and users consult the gap view weekly during planting months.
monetization: one-time — seasonal personal planning with no required external data feed.
constraints: Do not make climate, pesticide, or food-safety claims; use only user-defined crop durations in v1; portable local data.
why_distinct: A crop-turnover planner for one gardener’s real beds, not a CAD garden designer or generic gardening content app.

title: Phone Home Ops
user: A family member at home who needs a few shared actions—today’s task, location, note, and completion status—to work cleanly from a phone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A maker asked for feedback on a Flutter shared-home organizer, evidence that households still seek a shared operational surface beyond calendars and lists.
A household-management app reported that a new event cannot be closed on a phone, illustrating how desktop-shaped coordination tools fail at the point of use.

recurrence: A new shared-home product and a phone usability defect in another household tool both show the task is mobile, immediate, and easily lost in all-in-one dashboards.
current_workaround: Family chat, a note app, and an overloaded household organizer that is inconvenient to update while standing in a room.
incumbents_and_gap: Roomli, Neiliro, Cozi, and Notion offer broad spaces. The gap is a phone-first action strip where every card can be completed, deferred, or handed off in one thumb interaction.
smallest_useful_product: Local shared board of 3–12 action cards with assignee, room, due-today state, photo/note, QR device pairing, and append-only completion trail. Non-goals: calendar replacement, chat, finance, smart-home control, account administration.
success_measure: In a two-household test, 80% of cards created on mobile are resolved or rescheduled from mobile within seven days, with no desktop required.
monetization: one-time — a household utility should remain available without a hosted account.
constraints: Local-first device pairing and visible sync status; handle shared-device privacy; no surveillance-style activity scoring.
why_distinct: A deliberately narrow mobile execution surface, not a bundled household super-app.
